title: Neutrino Phone
one_liner: Compare light-speed latency through Earth's core versus around its surface between any two cities.
headline: Pick two cities and watch an honest physics race decide whether tunneling a neutrino beam straight through Earth's core actually beats today's surface-hugging fiber and satellite links.

episode.title: Why Altman Says "Accept Some Bad Things Happening" and What It Means for AI Safety | MOONSHOTS #301

history.summary: A clean, self-contained physics toy that nails the core idea: real haversine/chord geometry, accurate light-speed latency, an animated cutaway race, and unusually thorough honesty framing (tag, disclaimer, README "what's real" section, footer credit). The one loose thread is a duplicated, unused `data/cities.json` file and a label ("Through-core route") that slightly overstates how close the straight-line path actually gets to the core for nearby city pairs.

A clean, self-contained, zero-dependency prototype that computes exact great-circle vs. chord geometry from real city coordinates and renders it as a labeled cross-section race. The physics and disclaimers are unusually careful and internally consistent (percentages check out against the geometry), though the default city pair (NY–London) only shows a 3.2% saving, which undersells the idea's drama compared to more antipodal pairs.
reasons: A newer episode (steve-jurvetson-on-the-spacex-deal-that-almost-didn-t-happen-ep-314) revisits this topic: Pick two cities and race a fiber-optic route against a laser link between satellites in vacuum. (Jurvetson noted that light travels about 30% faster in a vacuum than in glass. Laser links between satellites also follow a straight path, unlike undersea cables that hug coastlines, so orbit can beat fiber on latency.)

A newer episode (ai-market-shocks-anthropic-s-stock-slide-gemini-releases-and-elon-s-435m-bet-314) revisits this topic: Race a data packet through undersea fiber against a laser relay through orbit between any two cities. (Steve explains that laser links between satellites beat fiber on the ground: light travels about 30% faster in vacuum than in glass, and space paths go straight instead of hugging coastlines.)
